title: Choose the next rung, not the roof
description: A goal becomes doable when you stop staring at the top and pick the one rung your hands can reach today.

body.heading: The roof is for direction, not for daily work
paragraphs: Big goals inspire from a distance and intimidate up close. Staring at the finished version — the fluent conversation, the finished book, the debt gone — while standing at the start can freeze people for months.
A ladder is a kinder picture. The roof tells you which way is up. But your hands only ever need the next rung, and the next rung is usually something refreshingly ordinary.

body.heading: Finding your next rung
paragraphs: Ask: what is the smallest step that would leave real evidence behind? Not “work on the novel” but “write the scene where they meet.” Not “get fit” but “walk to the park and back on Saturday.” Evidence matters because it proves the ladder is real and you are on it.
If you cannot name a rung that fits inside this week, the rungs are spaced too far apart. Break the step down until it fits. There is no rule that rungs must be impressive; they must be reachable.

body.heading: Climb, pause, look around
paragraphs: After each rung, a brief pause is part of the method: notice what changed, adjust the ladder if the wall turned out different than expected, then choose the next rung. Plans made from the ladder are better than plans made from the ground, because you can see more.

Some weeks the right move is to stay on your current rung and rest your arms. That still counts as being on the ladder. Falling off only happens when we decide the whole climb was a mistake — and one hard week is never that.

takeaway: Let the roof set the direction; let your hands choose only the next rung.
